title: Causes of the French Revolution
text:
The French Revolution began in 1789 and transformed France from an absolute monarchy into a republic. Historians usually group its causes into social, economic, political and intellectual factors, which together created a crisis that the old system could not survive.

French society under the Old Regime was divided into three estates. The First Estate was the clergy, and the Second Estate was the nobility. Together they made up less than three percent of the population, yet they owned a large share of the land and were mostly exempt from paying taxes. The Third Estate was everyone else, from wealthy merchants and lawyers to poor peasants and city workers. It made up about ninety-seven percent of the population and carried almost the entire tax burden. Peasants also had to pay feudal dues to their lords and a tithe to the Church.

The French state was close to bankruptcy by the 1780s. King Louis XVI had inherited large debts from earlier wars, and France spent heavily to support the American Revolution against Britain. The royal court at Versailles was also famously expensive, although its cost was small compared with the debt. Interest payments on loans took up around half of the government's spending. Attempts to reform taxes by making the nobles pay failed, because the nobility and the courts blocked them.

At the same time, ordinary people faced hardship. Poor harvests in 1788 caused the price of bread to rise sharply. Bread was the main food of the poor, and in Paris a worker could spend more than half of a day's wages on bread alone. Hunger made people angry and ready to protest.

New ideas also challenged the old order. Writers of the Enlightenment, such as Rousseau, Voltaire and Montesquieu, argued that power should come from the people, that all citizens should be equal before the law, and that government should be limited and divided. Educated members of the Third Estate read these ideas in pamphlets and discussed them in cafes and salons. The success of the American Revolution showed that such ideas could actually work.

To solve the financial crisis, Louis XVI called a meeting of the Estates-General in May 1789, the first since 1614. Each estate had one vote, so the clergy and nobles could always outvote the Third Estate. The representatives of the Third Estate demanded voting by head instead. When they were refused, they declared themselves the National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath, promising not to separate until France had a constitution. On 14 July 1789, crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, which became the symbol of the start of the Revolution.
keyPoints: French society was divided into three estates, and the clergy and nobles paid almost no taxes while the Third Estate carried the tax burden.
The French state was nearly bankrupt because of war debts, including support for the American Revolution.
Poor harvests in 1788 made the price of bread rise, causing hunger and anger.
Enlightenment writers such as Rousseau, Voltaire and Montesquieu argued for equality and power coming from the people.
Louis XVI called the Estates-General in 1789, and the Third Estate formed the National Assembly and swore the Tennis Court Oath.
Crowds stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789, marking the start of the Revolution.
